title: The Gurus' letters
hookLine: the Gurus sent signed letters to sangats, some still kept today

lines: AN OLD LETTER, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.
ADDRESSED TO A SANGAT BY NAME.
cards: A bundle wrapped in cloth, in a family's keeping or a gurdwara's care. Inside, an old sheet of paper, the ink faded, the creases gone soft. At the top, tradition says, a mark linked to the Guru's own hand.
Below it, lines addressed to a sangat in a faraway place, by name: a blessing, a thank-you, a request or two. Long ago it was carried in to a gathering and read aloud so that everyone could hear.
Then someone folded it, and decided it would be kept. Today's word: hukamnama.

teach.h: A LETTER OF THE GURU'S HUKAM.
teach.b: A hukamnama is a letter of hukam, the Guru's command, sent to a sangat. Hukam is a big word in Sikh teaching.

At the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that everything is within the divine hukam, the order of things, and nothing stands outside it. So a hukamnama was never just mail.
It carried the Guru's word to people who might never hear his voice. What did the letters say? Tradition and the surviving letters show a mix that's surprisingly human.
They bless the sangat. They thank it for offerings already sent. They ask for particular things the Guru's court needed.
They tell Sikhs to come when they can, to keep gathering, to live as Sikhs. Some carry the Guru's own signature or mark at the top.

And some of these letters are still kept today, held by families and gurdwaras with deep honor, because a letter like that is a link to the Guru's own hand. Here's the part that reaches into the present.
Today, in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and a hymn from the open page is read out.
That reading is also called the hukamnama, the day's word from the Guru.
At the Harmandir in Amritsar, the day's hukamnama is shared far beyond its walls. So the far-off sangat still waits for its letter. It just arrives every morning now, from the open page.

how: In gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and the hymn read from the page is called the hukamnama; the daily hukamnama from the Harmandir in Amritsar is widely shared, and historic hukamnamas of the Gurus are kept with honor.

games.q: you're in a far-off sangat, and a letter from the Guru has just arrived. what do you do with it?
o: read it aloud to the gathered sangat, then keep it with honor.
let the leader read it privately.
read it once and throw it away.
games.why: the letters were read to the sangat and kept, which is why some of them are still held today.

practice: Bring to mind one message someone sent you that you never threw away: a birthday card in a drawer, a note from a grandparent, a voicemail you haven't deleted.
Picture the handwriting, the voice, the first line, and ask what it said that still holds. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
